en: Now, last but not least, I mentioned that
you can also use Bun for testing, for unit
testing as a test runner. And therefore here
in this updated version of the project, I
added an index.test.ts file.
And in there you can see I'm importing
something from bun/test, from the test
package that's part of Bun.
Specifically, I'm importing some functions
you may know from other JavaScript unit
testing packages like Jest or Vitest.
Which allow me to set up tests and my test
conditions.
Now,
in this test.ts file, I got a little helper
function that creates a test request, a
dummy request, got a beforeEach function
that executes before each test to reset my
counter state. And then I got a test suite
here with individual tests. For example, a
test that renders that the current counter
value is rendered inside the HTML page. So I
call renderCounterPage here, which is just a
helper function in index.ts now, which
replaces that count placeholder in my
template with a counter value. And I test
whether that works correctly by evaluating
the generated HTML code and checking that
the correct counter value is output there.
Now, this is not a unit testing course. I
won't go through all that code in detail.
I will attach a detailed version with extra
comments though,
but this is all code that can be executed
with Bun. That doesn't require any extra
libraries or packages. That's the entire
point.
So I got these unit tests here that test
that the application behaves as intended.
And then in package.json, I got specific
test scripts.
And again, no extra dependencies, no Vitest,
Jest, or anything like that. Instead, using
built-in features and built-in tests.
Built-in commands, specifically the bun test
command.
So we have bun run for using the runtime for
executing code with Bun. We have bun build
for building. We have bun add and bun
install for adding packages and so on. And
then we got bun test to run tests, either
this command here to simply run all the
tests once, and by default it will simply
look for files that end with.test.ts or
.spec.ts.
Spec.ts,
or we run the tests in watch mode since
there is a supported --watch flag here too
so that tests are re-executed, rerun
whenever you change your code, or we
generate a coverage report to see how much
of our code is covered with tests.
So if I run bun test or bun run test to run
this script, though ironically, even if we
wouldn't have that script, we would run
bun test because test is simply a built-in
command. If I run bun test, it will simply
find all the test files in this project, run
them, and give me an overview here.
And testing is therefore the last important
capability of Bun because as mentioned, it's
mostly a runtime. That's what it's known
for. But it's also a very capable, secure,
and fast package manager, a build tool which
you can use for optimizing your code and for
making it production ready, and a test
runner, which allows you to set up and run
your unit tests without requiring any extra
libraries or packages.
